rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results sections report the authors' own coupled SWAP<U+2013>C2VSim model runs for a 3-year drought scenario (Tables 3<U+2013>7) and, in 'Estimates of agricultural idle land', their own NDVI/Landsat-based idle-cropland estimates (NASA and UC Davis) compared with the model (Table 8).
rows.notes: The study's core technology is a hydro-economic groundwater<U+2013>agricultural production model, not remote sensing. Remote sensing appears only as a cross-check: NDVI time series from MODIS/Landsat estimate an increase of about 212,700 ha of idle land in 2014 versus 2011 (95% classification accuracy against 670 field sites), and these estimates are shown to be broadly consistent with SWAP fallowing estimates (Table 8). This demonstrates that remote sensing can monitor/quantify drought-induced fallowing, a precondition for using it in policy, but the study reports no result showing that leveraging remote sensing in water policy confronts scarcity, climate change or competing demands (the claimed effect). The statement that Landsat data are helpful for refining model calibration (Discussion) is a recommendation, not a tested result. The authors themselves note that remote-sensing data measure total idle land, not fallowing attributable to drought. Stated limitations (survey-based water availability, no general-equilibrium effects, sub-regional variability masked) concern the economic model, not the remote-sensing claim.

notes: Full text appears complete (pages 1205<U+2013>1216). The paper is primarily a hydro-economic modelling study of groundwater substitution during the 2014 California drought; remote sensing is a secondary validation component, with the NASA idle-land estimates described as an ongoing effort by a coauthor's team.
